claims.text: MoNbTaW is a Ta-containing refractory BCC high-entropy alloy that can form a homogeneous solid solution.
The initial alloy is considered at temperatures near its melting point.
An MTP for MoNbTaW can be trained using DFT data from elemental, binary, ternary, and quaternary systems in the Nb-Ta-Mo-W chemical space.
The MTP training set should include explicit liquid-phase and high-temperature disordered configurations.
The proposed calculations should use 2000-3000 K, 1 atm, more than 1000 atoms, a 1 fs time step, a 4.7 Å MTP cutoff, and MTP level 14.
MTP uses contracted rotationally invariant moment-tensor descriptors that encode the chemical and angular structure of local atomic environments.
The MTP can capture variation associated with local chemical environments and short-range order in MoNbTaW.
The MTP captures the liquid structure of the multicomponent refractory alloy.
FEP calculates the relevant melting free-energy difference by exponential averaging of energy differences between solid and liquid states sampled with the MTP.
Using FEP avoids the slow convergence associated with full thermodynamic-integration paths.
MTP represents atomic energies as a polynomial or linear expansion in basis functions constructed from local moment-tensor descriptors.
MTP offers near-DFT accuracy with a favorable balance between accuracy and computational cost.
MTP-FEP will resolve melting free-energy differences within 5 meV/atom.
MTP-FEP will reduce computational cost by a factor of 10-100 relative to ab initio thermodynamic integration.
The resulting efficiency will enable high-throughput screening of Ta-based HEA compositions.
EAM potentials often fail to capture liquid structure in multicomponent systems.
The proposed model is valid within the Ta-Nb-Mo-W-V training-set chemical space but fails for extreme compositions or elements absent from training.
Omitting liquid configurations from training causes extrapolation artifacts and degraded liquid-state accuracy.
Sparse liquid-phase DFT training data may increase free-energy uncertainty by 20-50%.
A deviation greater than 10 meV/atom from direct AIMD thermodynamic integration is proposed as evidence that the apparent gain arises from training-set limitations.
